The latter two species suggest a Barremian age (J. F. Babinot, personal communication, 1989). Stratigraphically, the Hutubi Formation is part of the Tugulu Group, which according to Chen [1983] spans the entire early Cretaceous. The Hutubi Formation is overlain by the Shengjinkou Formation, itself overlain by the Lianmuqin Formation. In Wuerhe district, in the northwestern part of the Dzungar Basin, the Lianmuqin Formation has yielded a fairly varied vertebrate fauna [Dong, 1973] containing, among others, the dinosaur Psittacosaurus. Psittacosaurus is known in several other localities in Asia, from Siberia and Mongolia to northern China and Thailand [Buffetaut et al., 1989], in rocks which seem to correspond to the later part of the early Cretaceous (Aptian/Albian). The older Hutubi Formation is thus probably pre-Aptian in age. The strata outcrop on steeply dipping (>50 ø ) limbs of anticlines with roughly east-west fold axes (Figures. 2 and 3). They show that the AMS ellipsoid is oblate with minimum susceptibility normal to bedding and that the ratios of maximum to minimum susceptibility are rather high, averaging about 1.15. Indeed, we must address the question of whether these directions have suffered from compaction-induced inclination shallowing before the paleomagnetic inclinations can be interpreted in terms of paleolatitudes. This problem has recently been analyzed for natural sediments [Arason and Levi, 1990a], redeposited sediments [Levi and Banerjee, 1990], synthetic sediments [Dearner and Kodarna, 1990] or by numerical modeling [Arason and Levi, 1990b]. It appears that compaction of magnetite-bearing clay-rich deep-sea sediments may produce a significant inclination shallowing, as high as 15 ø , especially in the range 45o-60 ø of initial inclination. However, this phenomenon, which is not systematic in deep- sea sediments, is believed to be insignificant, if not absent, in quartz-rich sandstones [Dearner and Kodama, 1990; Starnatakos et al., 1989]. Because of the nature of the sediments in our study (coarse-grain continental sandstones), we believe that paleomagnetic inclinations parallel that of the GAD field within the range of experimental error. Sampled rocks are fine-grained sandstones with a pale red color. A total of 174 cores were sampled from 16 sites, 8 of which are on the northern limbs of the anticlines (Figure 3). PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS Minicores were collected with an electrically powered portable drill with standard 2.5-cm-diameter drill bits and were oriented with magnetic and Sun compasses. The average magnetic declination in the region of study is 4øW. In the laboratory the samples were cut into 2.2-cm-long specimens. Most magnetic measurements were carried out in the magnetically shielded room of the Paleomagnetic Laboratory at the Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris (IPGP), with a three-component cryogenic magnetometer. The remainder of measurements were done at the Paleomagnetic Laboratory of the Universit6 de Rennes (UR), using a single axis cryogenic magnetometer and a Schonstedt spinner flux gate magnetometer. A total of 282 specimens were measured. The intensities of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) ranged from 1 to 200 mA/m, averaging 2 mA/m. Most specimens were thermally demagnetized, in the laboratory-built furnace at the IPGP and in a Schonstedt furnace at the UR, and several specimens were demagnetized by alternating field (af). We carefully selected the region and the sedimentary series to be sampled. The Lisboa region seems to fulfill a lot of these requirements (Fig. 1). Some deformation occurred also during the emplacement of the intrusive Sintra Massif, and the Tertiary. Sedimentary facies of outer platform prevailed before the late Bar- remian. Geology, Academia Sinica, Beijing (China) Received 15 May 1988; revised version received January 23, 1989 More than 150 oriented samples were collected along the Kaxigal-Lhasa road in the southwestern part of the Tibetan Plateau to determine the deformation aspect of the Tibetan region from a paleomagnetic point of view. The counter-clockwise deflection about 60 o in declination was revealed at four localities in the narrow zone along the Indus-Zangbo suture zone. A north to northeast direction (D = -9 ° to 30 o) was observed at four localities, more than 14 km from the suture zone in the western Tibetan region. Significant tectonic deformation has occurred exclusively in a narrow zone whose width is about 40 km spanning the suture zone. The crustal blocks of this narrow zone were rotated in a compressive regime accompanied by left-lateral shear during the collision of the Indo-Eurasia continents. The deformation of the narrow zone behaves as a buffer zone in a tectonically gigantic dimension where the tangential stress is mainly absorbed. 1. Introduction The Indian continent moved northward since its splitting from Antarctica and collided with the Eurasian continent at about 50 Ma [1,2]. Introduction The Indian continent moved northward since its splitting from Antarctica and collided with the Eurasian continent at about 50 Ma [1,2]. Its colli- sion and subsequent indentation toward the Eura- sian continent have given rise to internal deforma- tion in the southern part of Eurasia [3]. Because the Tibetan region has behaved as a bumper against the northward rush of India since 50 Ma [2,4-6], there is abundant geological evidence con- cerning tectonic deformation preserved in this re- gion. The Tibetan region thus provides a magnifi- cent opportunity to study the deformation of con- tinents. Paleomagnetism offers a quantitative method for establishing the geological aspect of the defor- mation of continents. was concentrated in the Aksu-Keping area on the northwestern margin of the Tarim block (see Fig. 2). The structures sam- pied are gently dipping sequences spanning Cambrian to Lower Permian time continuously, except for a few disconformities. The stratigraphic column is repeated by a series of southwest- northeast striking, apparently southeast-vergent thrust faults. The lithologies are suggestive of a stable platform depositional environment: Cam- brian and Ordovician units are carbonates with shallow water marine fauna (primarily trilobites). Silurian deposits are thin where present, and con- sist of green marine, argillaceous sandstone, fol- lowed by spectacular exposures of Devonian fluvial/alluvial red sandstone up to 2000 m in stratigraphic thickness. A major disconformity 277 separates the Devonian rocks from Upper Carboniferous shallow water marine limestones abundant with coral, and interbedded mature, well-sorted sandstone layers [18]. Ortega- Gutierrez [11] suggests that the evidence from the Acatlan Complex indicates a collisional mid- Paleozoic orogeny, associated with the closure of a Lower Paleozoic ocean possibly related to the Proto-Atlantic or Iapetus ocean. The suture is inferred to lie at the present contact between the Oaxaca and Acatlan complexes. Also included in the Acatlan Complex is a cataclastic complex of undifferentiated granitoids with metasediment intercalations (Esperanza Granitoids), a trondhjemitic pluton (Totoltepec Granite) which has been deformed and slightly metamorphosed [10] and a swarm of undeformed dikes (San Miguel Dikes). (Mexico) Received September 22, 1988; revised version received May 25, 1989 232 drill samples were collected from 33 sites from the Acatlan Terrane, southern Mexico. The medium-grade metamorphosed basement rocks (schists, granitoid, greenstones) showed magnetic directions that are randomly distributed and no meaningful results could be obtained. However, late Paleozoic red beds, the Ordovician (?) Totoltepec Granite and the early Paleozoic (?) Tecomate Limestone (metamorphosed in Acadian times) give coherent paleomagnetic directions. The samples responded well to thermal demagnetization but not to alternating field demagnetization. The ages of the magnetizations are reasonably bracketed between Carboniferous and Jurassic. Compared with data from the North American craton and from the Oaxaca terrane, conclusive evidence for major north-south displacements of the Acatlan terrane is not present, but significant clockwise rotations of the terrane with respect to the craton and the adjacent Oaxaca terrane are quite evident. These rotations occurred during the Jurassic or Early Cretaceous. 1. Introduction The paleogeographical position of the basement blocks of Mexico has been an enigma for years. Paleomagnetic results and analysis Samples were cut into 2.2 cm high specimens (2.5 cm diameter) and then measured in the paleomagnetic laboratory at the University of 134 Michigan, using a two-axis ScT cryogenic magne- tometer. Both alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetizations were performed with Schonstedt equipment. Components of magnetization were identified by visual inspection of orthogonal vec- tor diagrams [18], and their directions were determined by principal component analysis [19]. Natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) and demagnetization results from the schists (Cosol- tepec Formation), greenstones and granitoid (Esperanza Formation), Triassic dikes (San Miguel Dikes) and Jurassic sediments are disappointing: the magnetic directions are generally randomly distributed and there is no consistency either within or between site(s). They are excluded from further analysis. In contrast, specimens from the Totoltepec Granite, Tecomate Limestone and "Matzitzi equivalent" red beds all yield coherent paleomagnetic directions. The paleodirection associated with this remagnetization is consistent with the contention that Thailand was a part of Eurasia at that time and that it has suffered some 20 o of clockwise rotation subsequently. Also consistent is the observed azimuthal difference of Mesozoic fold axes on either side of the Red River fault, as is the early geometry of and sense of motion on this fault. Re-interpretation of late Neogene data suggests that rotation may have continued into the Neogene. The clustering of in situ directions (Fig. 4a) strongly suggests that magneti- zation was acquired after the tectonic events that induced folding. A further indication that remagnetization in- deed occurred is given by results from site 5 (Triassic basal conglomerate), in which samples were drilled both from the coarse-grained Triassic sandstone matrix and pebbles of Permian lime- stone. The characteristic directions from all cores are in close agreement, and the overall mean has an ot95 of 4.5 °. Clearly, this implies a negative conglomerate test and further makes it doubtful that the underlying Permian rocks now carry a primary magnetization. Based on a marginally positive foldtest, Achache and Courtillot sug- gested that the magnetization might be Triassic. The test [7, fig. 4], however, relied almost entirely on the poorest determined direction, that of site 8. Given our additional data, the Triassic sites no longer provide a positive foldtest; on the contrary, the ot95 for Triassic sites increases when site 8 is excluded and the foldtest is negative at the 95% confidence level (Table 1). There is therefore little doubt that all of the sites reported in this paper and in Achache and Courtillot [7] have been remagnetized after the Triassic. The single Jurassic site reported here suggests that the remagnetization event may be considerably younger (Figs. 4 and 6).

Following the intrusion of the Mbabane and other related plutons, such as the Mpageni, Ngwempisi and Sinceni (Fig. l), the area of east- em Kaapvaal craton has had a very quiet tectonic and thermal history [17] with the exception of an episode of dike emplacement between 2000 and 2300 Ma [18] and eruption of Karoo lavas in the Mesozoic. Previous paleomagnetic work in north- central Swaziland had yielded a 2875 + 40 Ma (Rb-Sr and Sm-Nd isochron ages) pole from the mafic-ultramafic Usushwana Complex [19]. We compare the pole from the Mbabane Pluton with that from the Usushwana Complex in an attempt to identify the existence of apparent polar wander in the late Archean in southern Africa. 2. Geologic summary The Mbabane Pluton is a coarse-grained porphyritic granitic pluton of high topographic relief located in north-central Swaziland east of Mbabane (Fig. 1). The pluton is exposed as a tear-drop shaped structure 35 km long with a maximum width of 18 km. Medium-granted bio- tite-rich inclusions are common in this pluton and appear to be disc-shaped and randomly oriented [20]. The pluton intrudes gneisses and migmatites of the Ancient Gneiss Complex in the south, and homogeneous massive adamellites of the Mpuluzi Batholith in the north [17] (Fig. 1). ut 65 ° different from that of the Usushwana Complex, while the sites are only 12 km apart. There are no known faults between the two bodies or rotations of either body which could account for this difference in pole positions [20,21]. In addition, the higher temperature magnetic di- rection seen in the Mbabane Pluton is also pre- sent, with the same direction, as an overprint in Usushwana Complex samples [19], implying no relative rotation between these two bodies since the intrusion of the Mbabane Pluton. These two well dated paleomagnetic poles from Swaziland, then, provide the first direct evidence that there was significant apparent polar wander, and hence cratonal motion of the Kaapvaal Craton, in the late Archean. Structural explanations The Koipato magnetic discordance consists mainly of a roughly 20 ° steepening of inclination (95% error limits about 10°). Thus the discor- dance would be nicely accounted for if the rocks had accumulated on a regional southward slope of about 20 °, instead of a horizontal surface. This is the troublesome "original dip" problem of paleomagnetism, which in many cases can be overcome simply by sampling over an area large enough to average out paleotopographic irregular- ities. Unfortunately, we have data for only a fairly restricted part of a single mountain range. An examination of situations where basalt flows occur suggests that original dips of 20 ° are perhaps a bit extreme, but that in worst-case scenarios 15 ° is possible. For instance, south slopes of modern Cascade volcanos reach 16-17 ° but average somewhat less. Shield volcanos have much lower slopes (e.g., the 1929 flow on the south flank of Mauna Loa flowed down a slope of slightly less than 7°). The maximum regional slope down east-facing scarps in the Death Valley area is about 15 ° , but the average is much less. Maxi- mum slopes into most sedimentary basins are very small. In

A discussion of the tectonic signifi- cance of these data will follow (R.C. Speed, manuscript in preparation). 4.1. Geomagnetic explanations Possibly the least likely explanation for the discordance is that our mean direction has not averaged non-dipole elements of the geomagnetic field, and thus cannot be compared directly to dipole directions for the craton. We cannot esti- mate the time-interval represented by our 11 flows, but they span at least one polarity transition, are spread over a reasonably large geographical area, and have scatter characteristics similar to other paleomagnetic data sets that average the non-di- pole field. The shape of the data set (and a con- sistency-of-reversal t~st) argue that we have not sampled an excursion or polarity transition. Thus, baring some highly improbable (and essentially untestable) abberation of the geomagnetic field, the Koipato discordance is caused by geology, not geomagnetism. 4.2. The most likely explanation for this discordance is southward transport and clockwise rotation of the sampling area. The most probable amount of displacement and net rotation are 1400 km and 25 °, respectively. These observations have considerable significance for the early Mesozoic tectonics of the Great Basin. 1. Introduction The Mesozoic tectonics of western Nevada has been a subject of long debate, and continues to have considerable significance in discussions of the evolution of the North American continental margin and the histories of accreted terranes [1-6]. Much discussion centers on the nature and timing of the early Mesozoic Sonoma orogeny. We have obtained paleomagnetic results that provide some useful constraints. The Sonoma orogeny is the oldest recognized tectonic event of probable Mesozoic age in west- ern Nevada (Fig. 1). The Sonoma orogeny is dated by deformed rocks as young as Guadelupian within the Golconda allochthon, and by the existence of an unconformity at the base of Triassic strata that cover the deformed Golconda rocks. The basal unit of the cover sequence is

9 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. During the Sonoma orogeny the Golconda al- lochthon was displaced at least 80 km eastward across the edge of North America. Major ques- tions about the emplacement of the Golconda allochthon include: (1) was it far travelled before emplacement [31, or was it locally derived [2]; (2) was it emplaced in Early Triassic or Late Permian time, before deposition of its Triassic cover [3], or was it emplaced together with its cover in post- Triassic time [5]? We reasoned that by obtaining paleolatitude data for the Koipato and other cover rocks, we might help answer these questions. To this end we have sampled and studied over 500 samples (about 60 sites) from two general areas in western Nevada. However, the difficulties of doing paleomagnetism in a multiply-deformed, much-in- truded terrain are such that to date we have reliable results only from 11 sites in a single (Koipato) formation. The Koipato data are pre- sented here; preliminary results for the remaining formations are reported in two theses [9,10]. Work on the latter rocks is still in progress. 2. A rotating block domain model in which north-south compression is super- imposed on WNW-ESE strike-slip faults in SW Puerto Rico can explain the inferred rotation. Introduction Studies from a variety of geologic disciplines indicate that the Northem Car

o use paleomagnetism in the structurally complex region of southwest Puerto Rico to determine the sense and magnitude of crustal/lithospheric block rotations relative to North America. Pre-Oligocene paleomagnetism is of particular interest because a major change in relative mo- tions took place in the Eocene among the Caribbean, North American and South American plates (e.g. Malfait and Dinkel- man, 1972; Pindell and Dewey, 1982; Burke et al., 1984; Duncan and Hargraves, 1984). Sheriff Department of Geology, University of Montana, Missoula Abstract. Twelve virtual geomagnetic poles from 25 paleomagnetic sites in the Oligocene Hog Heaven volcanic field of northwestern Montana yield a mean pole at 74.4øN, 71.5øE (alpha 95 = 5.9ø). This pole indicates clockwise rotation of 10.5 ø +_ 7.4 ø and flattening of 13.2 ø + 4.6 ø at the 95% confidence level. Assuming the axial geocentric dipole hypothesis criteria have been satisfied, at 95% confidence rotation and flattening are statistically different from zero. These results indicate clockwise rotation of the Hog Heaven volcanic field as expected for the Sanpoil block farther west. However under these assumptions this farsided pole requires northward transport of nearly 1400 km, about 100 time

unding the basins are active and structurally adequate to accommodate the rotation of the Sanpoll volcanic field. The Hog Heaven volcanic field lies between these basins and the Sanpoil volcanic field. The Hog Heaven volcanic field is well positioned to determine if the post 40 mybp rotation of the Sanpoil block also affects the Purcell anticlinorium. These rocks appear to be ideal for such a study as: 1) they span 5 million years, 2) there are interbedded sediments, 3) reverse and normal polarities are recorded by the rocks, 4) numerous lithologies are present, and 5) the rocks are relatively flat lying. However, 25 paleomagnetic sites yielded only 12 reliable virtual geomagnetic poles (VGP) from the Hog Heaven volcanic field. Despite the favorable geologic relations, the 12 VGP do not yield a reasonable estimate of the Oligocene rotation axis. Field and Lab Procedures and Paleomagnetic Results At each of 25 outcrops, roadcuts, or mine shafts in the Hog Heaven volcanic field, about eight independently oriented 2.5 cm cores were collected using a portable drill, a magnetic compass, and where possible a sun compass. Local deflections of the magnetic compass caused by the outcrop were never more than a few degrees, none of the sites had results suggestive of extensive remagnetization by lightning strikes. There is no large scale magnetic anomaly associated with the Hog Heaven volcanic field or the associated silver mineralization. The rock types sampled include lava flows, small dacitic intrusions, welded ash flows, and dikes. The Hog Heaven rocks spent the past 30 million years weathering near the earth's surface, they are not particularly well exposed. Several recent papers favor the idea that many of the blocks were derived from Paleozoic Gondwanaland, with later northward movements as one after the other accreted to the Asian continent [e.g., Audley-Charles et al., 1988]. With tM Siberian nucleus of Asia in more northerly Paleozoic palcolatitudes and Gondwana situated over the south pole, palcomagnetism is ideally suited as a technique to test Paleozoic paleogeographic models and the later northward drift of tach blocks as Tarim, Indochina, North and South China. In this paper we report on a paleomagnetic study of two feintions: the Ordovician Daqing and Hongshiya formations, mllected from the area near Kunming (Figure 1). Located at the southwestern end of the Yangtze Paraplatform (SCB), this area remained a stable platform experiencing only minor vertical movements for about 600 million years (late Precambrian to late Mesozoic), unlike other pans of the paraplafform where the Caledonian and Yanshanian (Jurassic) oregenies had profound effects. Several recent papers favor the idea that many of the blocks were derived from Paleozoic Gondwanaland, with later northward movements as one after the other accreted to the Asian continent [e.g., Audley-Charles et al., 1988]. With tM Siberian nucleus of Asia in more northerly Paleozoic palcolatitudes and Gondwana situated over the south pole, palcomagnetism is ideally suited as a technique to test Paleozoic paleogeographic models and the later northward drift of tach blocks as Tarim, Indochina, North and South China. In this paper we report on a paleomagnetic study of two feintions: the Ordovician Daqing and Hongshiya formations, mllected from the area near Kunming (Figure 1). Located at the southwestern end of the Yangtze Paraplatform (SCB), this area remained a stable platform experiencing only minor vertical movements for about 600 million years (late Precambrian to late Mesozoic), unlike other pans of the paraplafform where the Caledonian and Yanshanian (Jurassic) oregenies had profound effects. The Iznalloz section (Betic cordillera, Spain) provides a continuous outcrop (20 m thick) of Toarcian ammonitico rosso limestones with all the ammonite zones defined in the Boric realm. The characteristic magnetization direction for each sample was obtained by detailed thermal demagnetization and was stable from about 450 to 560øC. The magnetic polarity sequence extends from the Polymorphum to the Aalensis ammonite zone, and covers the whole Toareian stage. Thus this section presents a good pattern of the reversal succession during Toarcian times. Considering hiatuses of sampling and excluding single-sample magnetozones, there does not seem to be any important change in the reversal rate during this period. On the north coast, the deposition of shallow-water carbonates with a minor clastic component was nearly continuous from late Oligocene through Neogene, interrupted by an unconformity during the late Miocene. These units have remained essentially undisturbed structurally, dipping northward four to eight degrees toward the Puerto Rico Trench, where the units become slightly thicker [Monroe, 1980; Seiglie and Moussa, 1984; Moussa et al., 1987]. On the north coast, the deposition of shallow-water carbonates with a minor clastic component was nearly continuous from late Oligocene through Neogene, interrupted by an unconformity during the late Miocene. These units have remained essentially undisturbed structurally, dipping northward four to eight degrees toward the Puerto Rico Trench, where the units become slightly thicker [Monroe, 1980; Seiglie and Moussa, 1984; Moussa et al., 1987]. Introduction Palcomagnetism has proved to be a useful tool to unravel the complex sequence of relative motions and collisions of the many blocks that together form the Asian mosaic (e.g., North China Block (NCB), South China Block (SCB), Tarim and the numerous accreted terranes of the Tibetan region)(Figure 1). Late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic formations have been intensively studied by modern palcomagnetic methods since 1981 (e.g. McElhinny et al., 1981). The collision of the NCB and SCB was suggested on that basis to have taken place between the Middle Triassic and the Middle Jurassic (Lin, 1984; Zhao and Coe, 1987). The precise timing of complete suturing was not well constrained due to the scarcity of reliable results for the middle to late Mesozoic and to the major problem of widespread late Mesozoic to recent remagnetization in eastern China (e.g., Kent et al., 1987; Zhao et al., 1990; Huang and Opdyke, 1991). Introduction Palcomagnetism has proved to be a useful tool to unravel the complex sequence of relative motions and collisions of the many blocks that together form the Asian mosaic (e.g., North China Block (NCB), South China Block (SCB), Tarim and the numerous accreted terranes of the Tibetan region)(Figure 1). Late Paleozoic and early Mesozoic formations have been intensively studied by modern palcomagnetic methods since 1981 (e.g. McElhinny et al., 1981). The collision of the NCB and SCB was suggested on that basis to have taken place between the Middle Triassic and the Middle Jurassic (Lin, 1984; Zhao and Coe, 1987). The precise timing of complete suturing was not well constrained due to the scarcity of reliable results for the middle to late Mesozoic and to the major problem of widespread late Mesozoic to recent remagnetization in eastern China (e.g., Kent et al., 1987; Zhao et al., 1990; Huang and Opdyke, 1991). A more detailed rock magnetic analysis of the samples, therefore, was conducted. The acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) is a common technique aiding the identification of ferromagnetic mineral content. Interpretation of IRM acquisition curves, however, can be ambiguous since some ferromagnetic minerals, such as goethite and hematite, can have similar coercivities [Heller, 1978; Lowtie and Heller, 1982]. Stepwise thermal demagnetization of an IRM can resolve such ambiguities since many minerals which have similar maximum coercivities have different unblocking temperatures [Heller, 1978]. Recently, a modification of the thermal demagnetization of IRM has been presented providing even greater resolution of ferromagnetic mineral content, especially in relatively weakly magnetized pelagic limestones [Lowale, 1990]. Recently, a modification of the thermal demagnetization of IRM has been presented providing even greater resolution of ferromagnetic mineral content, especially in relatively weakly magnetized pelagic limestones [Lowale, 1990]. ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION OF THE COMPONENTS OF MAGNETIZATION Origin and Timing of the A component In almost every site, the A component is well identified with low to intermediate unblocking temperatures. Combinations of demagnetization techniques suggest that the A component probably resides in magnetite in all cases (although components with unblocking temperatures less than 580øC do not preclude hematite). In some sites that are closely spaced, sometimes even within a site, the unblocking temperatures for the A component vary greatly. This would be very difficult to explain in terms of a simple thermal overprint other than a chemical remagnetization (or a combination of chemical and other processes), because, in the former case, the unblocking temperature should remain more or less the same. Among these blocks, the North China Block (NCB) is of particular interest in understanding the tectonic history of Asia because of its large area and central position in east Asia. Paleomagnetic data from the NCB would not only provide constraints on the tectonic history of the block itself but also on the overall geologic history and paleogeographic reconstruction of Asia. Zhang et al., 1984; Yang et al., 1986], no strong constraints on the locations of the NCB during most of Paleozoic time are available. We reported two preliminary Cambrian and Ordovician paleomagnetic poles for the NCB from our own preliminary studies at several meetings [Zhao and Coe, 1985; Zhao et al., 1989], and gave a tentative interpretation of them in a thesis [Zhao, 1987]. In this paper, we present the detailed account of our paleomagnetic results, including those from many new measurements, derived from Latest Precambrian-Early Cambrian to Middle Ordovician shale, limestone, and dolomite from three widely separated localities in Hebei and Shandong provinces. Because our data pass the fold, baked contact, and reversal tests, we believe that the magnetization may be primary, with little or no contamination by unremoved secondary remanent magnetization. We then compare other relevant paleomagnetic data from China and discuss the tectonic and paleogeographic implications. ANALYSIS AND DISCUSSION OF THE COMPONENTS OF MAGNETIZATION Origin and Timing of the A component In almost every site, the A component is well identified with low to intermediate unblocking temperatures. Combinations of demagnetization techniques suggest that the A component probably resides in magnetite in all cases (although components with unblocking temperatures less than 580øC do not preclude hematite). In some sites that are closely spaced, sometimes even within a site, the unblocking temperatures for the A component vary greatly. This would be very difficult to explain in terms of a simple thermal overprint other than a chemical remagnetization (or a combination of chemical and other processes), because, in the former case, the unblocking temperature should remain more or less the same. Among these blocks, the North China Block (NCB) is of particular interest in understanding the tectonic history of Asia because of its large area and central position in east Asia. Paleomagnetic data from the NCB would not only provide constraints on the tectonic history of the block itself but also on the overall geologic history and paleogeographic reconstruction of Asia. The faunas have a strong Tethyan affinity and the late Permian flora contains typical Cathaysiopteris, implying a relatively close relation between the Qamdo Block and the South China (Yangtze) Block during the late Paleozoic. A prefolding Cretaceous direction derived from 14 sites along the Xinjiang-Tibet highway yielded a rather low paleolatitude of 10.9 ø +-- 3.0 ø for a reference at Domar (33.7øN, 80.4øE) [Chen et al., 1991b] but indicated little rotation relative to eratonic Eurasia (Y. Chen, personal communication, 1991). Another study was carried out by Pozzi and Feinberg [1991] on the Lower Cretaceous red beds from the Tajik basin (38.6øN, 68.9øE). They isolated a stable and well-defined magnetization from most samples of all four sites and a second direction of high unblocking temperatures and reversed polarity from several samples of one site. They interpreted the former as a prefolding remagnetization and the latter as a primary direc- tion. The results suggested a counterclockwise rotation of 26 ø - 9 ø for the sampled area, and insignificant (probably 100-300 km) postcollision crustal shortening north of the Tajik basin. The faunas have a strong Tethyan affinity and the late Permian flora contains typical Cathaysiopteris, implying a relatively close relation between the Qamdo Block and the South China (Yangtze) Block during the late Paleozoic. Two sets of paleomagnetic data were recently reported from the Lower Cretaceous rocks on the eastern and west- ern sides of the Pamir (Western) Syntaxis [Chen et al., 1991b; Pozzi and Feinberg, 1991]. A prefolding Cretaceous direction derived from 14 sites along the Xinjiang-Tibet highway yielded a rather low paleolatitude of 10.9 ø +-- 3.0 ø for a reference at Domar (33.7øN, 80.4øE) [Chen et al., 1991b] but indicated little rotation relative to eratonic Eurasia (Y. Chen, personal communication, 1991). Another study was carried out by Pozzi and Feinberg [1991] on the Lower Cretaceous red beds from the Tajik basin (38.6øN, 68.9øE). They isolated a stable and well-defined magnetization from most samples of all four sites and a second direction of high unblocking temperatures and reversed polarity from several samples of one site. They interpreted the former as a prefolding remagnetization and the latter as a primary direc- tion. The results suggested a counterclockwise rotation of 26 ø - 9 ø for the sampled area, and insignificant (probably 100-300 km) postcollision crustal shortening north of the Tajik basin. A general picture outlined by the existing paleomagnetic data appears to be that immediately north of the Indian indenter the continental crust was substantially shortened in a north-south direction. dle Cretaceous redbed formations from eastern Qiangtang Terrane, Tibet. The tilt-corrected mean direction for the Lower Cretaceous is D/I = 57.70/50.2 ø with a95 = 10.9 ø and N = 12 sites, and that for the Middle Cretaceous is D/I = 39.7ø/51.6 ø with a95 -- 8.5 ø and N = 11 sites. Both formations pass the fold test, and the latter possesses two polarities. The magnetization predates the Eocene and was probably acquired during Cretaceous time. Comparison of the mean directions with expected directions from the stable interior of Eurasia indicates significant clockwise rotation but little paleolatitudinal change for the sampling area. Deformation and rotation of these rocks are presumably related to the collision of India with Asia and its subsequent northward indentation into Asia. Existing paleomagnetic data from Tibet and its environs seems to be compatible with a crustal shortening/thickening model (Dewey et al., 1988) in that the continental crust directly north of the Indian indenter was substantially shortened north-south, whereas in the vicinity of the Western and Eastern Syntaxes, latitudinal displacement was minimal but tectonic rotation was very important. More data are needed to further differentiate between this model and the lateral eastward crustal extrusion mode

In unmetamorphosed rocks the bulk of the iron (=1-4 wt % in whole rock) occurs as surfides. The bituminous rocks are also enriched in Ni and Cr. The gradual oxidation of Fe, which has not been mobilized, as well as the oxidation and subsequent mobilization into veins of Cr and Ni, are the most visually striking aspects of metamorphism. The typical medium-grade rock forming mineral in the MZ is spurrite, with minor brownmillerite. In these rocks the Fe-phase is in most cases an oxide, usually maghemite. Relict greigite has been observed in some black colored spurrites. With increasing grade, larnite becomes a significant phase. The highest grade common rocks in the MZ are gehlenite- garnet (shorlomite)-pyroxene fels rocks. These contain hematite, often magnetite, and, in one case, Ni or Ti bearing chromite. Fission-track dating of the Maale Adumim outcrop [Kolodny et al., 1971] suggests that burning at this site took place in the Middle Miocene (13.6 + 2Ma). When natural combustion occurs in bituminous marine sediments, the temperature increase and the ignition of the organic material is often the consequence of low temperature oxidation of finely disseminated framboidal pyrite, a frequent component of such rocks [Mathews and Bustin, 1984]. The \"Mottled Zone\" (MZ) complex (formally termed the Hatrurim Formation) is a sequence of CM rocks in Israel and Jordan, cropping out in several localities, the largest of which are the Hatrurim basin (near Arad), the Maale Adumim area on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho, and the Daba-Siwaqa area south of Amman (Figure 1). The unmetamorphosed protoliths were the bituminous rocks of the Cretaceous Ghareb and Early Tertiary Taqiye Formations. These are well bedded bituminous chalks and marls, and some phosphorites. Rocks of both of these formations contain large amounts of iron sulfides, both as dispersed microcrystalline pyrite and as pyrite concretions, up to several centimeters in diameter. The typical natural remanent magnetization (NRM) intensity of such protoliths is on the order of 10-4A/m; the detrital component in these rocks is negligible, and no significant amount of detrital magnetite has been detected in them. The metamorphic rocks are characterized by the disappearance of sedimentary bedding, strong veining, and \"mottling\" in color; red-green-yellow-b

are the most visually striking aspects of metamorphism. The typical medium-grade rock forming mineral in the MZ is spurrite, with minor brownmillerite. In these rocks the Fe-phase is in most cases an oxide, usually maghemite. Relict greigite has been observed in some black colored spurrites. With increasing grade, larnite becomes a significant phase. The highest grade common rocks in the MZ are gehlenite- garnet (shorlomite)-pyroxene fels rocks. These contain hematite, often magnetite, and, in one case, Ni or Ti bearing chromite. Fission-track dating of the Maale Adumim outcrop [Kolodny et al., 1971] suggests that burning at this site took place in the Middle Miocene (13.6 + 2Ma). Stratigraphic evidence suggests that metamorphism at Hatrurim basin is younger than the Miocene Hazeva Formation [Kolodny et al., 1973]. Detailed mapping, preliminary K-At dating (D. Zur, personal communication, 1991) and preliminary electron spin resonance dating (N. Porat, personal communication, 1991) suggest that the burning in the Hatrurim area has been even younger, maybe late Pliocene [Burg et al., 1992]. B4, PAGES 4331-4348, APRIL 10, 1992 FURTHER STUDIES OF CARBONATE REMAGNETIZATION IN THE NORTHERN APPALACHIAN BASIN Barbara Saffer and Chad McCabe Department of Geology and Geophysics, Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge Abstract. Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic studies of sedimentary carbonates in the northern Appalachian Basin demonstrate that the late Paleozoic remagnetization in this area is probably related to authigenesis of single- domain magnetite. Fifteen sites within Middle Devonian carbonates were sampled along a transect extending from Albany, New York, to the Algonquin Arch in southeastern Ontario. Paleomagnetic studies show that all sites except the two westernmost sites on the Algonquin Arch were remagnetized during Alleghenian time. The very weakly magnetic unremagnetized sites retain a dual-polarity magnetization of probable Devonian age. In the remagnetized sites, both the size of the Kiaman components and magnetite concentration, estimated from low-field susceptibility (X), are highest in the central part of the transect and lower on either side. uisiana State University, Baton Rouge Abstract. Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic studies of sedimentary carbonates in the northern Appalachian Basin demonstrate that the late Paleozoic remagnetization in this area is probably related to authigenesis of single- domain magnetite. Fifteen sites within Middle Devonian carbonates were sampled along a transect extending from Albany, New York, to the Algonquin Arch in southeastern Ontario. Paleomagnetic studies show that all sites except the two westernmost sites on the Algonquin Arch were remagnetized during Alleghenian time. The very weakly magnetic unremagnetized sites retain a dual-polarity magnetization of probable Devonian age. In the remagnetized sites, both the size of the Kiaman components and magnetite concentration, estimated from low-field susceptibility (X), are highest in the central part of the transect and lower on either side. X ray powder diffraction analyses demonstrate that K-feldspar is also most abundant in the middle of the transect, with lower concentrations to the west and east. We suggest that formation of authigenic magnetite and K-feldspar may be related in this setting. Sites with the largest Kiaman components have the highest unblocking temperatures and the largest ratios of anhysteretic

particles. A majority of the magnetite grains contain Fe as the only cation, but many also contain minor amounts of other cations including various combinations of Cr, Ni, Ti, Zn, Mn, Si, A1, Ca, and Mg. Single- domain magnetite is not resolvable with our observational techniques, but its presence is inferred from rock magnetic tests. Much of this magnetite may be of authigenic origin. uisiana State University, Baton Rouge Abstract. Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic studies of sedimentary carbonates in the northern Appalachian Basin demonstrate that the late Paleozoic remagnetization in this area is probably related to authigenesis of single- domain magnetite. Fifteen sites within Middle Devonian carbonates were sampled along a transect extending from Albany, New York, to the Algonquin Arch in southeastern Ontario. Paleomagnetic studies show that all sites except the two westernmost sites on the Algonquin Arch were remagnetized during Alleghenian time. The very weakly magnetic unremagnetized sites retain a dual-polarity magnetization of probable Devonian age. In the remagnetized sites, both the size of the Kiaman components and magnetite concentration, estimated from low-field susceptibility (X), are highest in the central part of the transect and lower on either side. X ray powder diffraction analyses demonstrate that K-feldspar is also most abundant in the middle of the transect, with lower concentrations to the west and east. We suggest that formation of authigenic magnetite and K-feldspar may be related in this setting. Sites with the largest Kiaman components have the highest unblocking temperatures and the largest ratios of anhysteretic

particles. A majority of the magnetite grains contain Fe as the only cation, but many also contain minor amounts of other cations including various combinations of Cr, Ni, Ti, Zn, Mn, Si, A1, Ca, and Mg. Single- domain magnetite is not resolvable with our observational techniques, but its presence is inferred from rock magnetic tests. Much of this magnetite may be of authigenic origin. The Devonian 40Ar-39Ar biotite age of 370 Ma reported by Mitchell and Roberts (1986) repre- sented a total fusion age, and yielded ‘a complex age spectrum with no clear plateau at any true statistical significance’. It has been demonstrated in this account that titanomagnetites, with block- ing-temperatures up to 550-580 o C, crystallized/ recrystallized in Permian times. If a Devonian age for the Ytteroy dyke is accepted, it is most surpris- ing that ‘Devonian’ biotites with blocking-temper- atures of say - 300” C were not reset, whereas titanomagnetites with substantially higher block- ing-temperatures suffered complete overprinting. In conclusion, unless the HB component is exclu- sively secondary and thermo-chemical in origin, and this is most unlikely, we must consider that the Rb-Sr age of 256 * 10 reflects the initial cooling system of the dyke, and is compatible with the Ytteroy HB component. The apparently high 40Ar-39Ar age may be ascribed to excess Ar, pre- sumably related to late Mesozoic hydrothermal alteration. It is also possible that such later hydro- thermal alteration may induce K-loss, which would have the effect of giving an anomalously high 40Ar-39Ar age (J.R. Magnetic structure and evolution of the island of Santa Maria, Azores. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 58: 228—238. A palaeomagnetic study of the major volcanic units of Santa Maria reveals dominantly reverse characteristic magnetizations with a mean direction of D = 179, I = —49 and 095 = 2.1° (85 specimens from 20 sites). Sporadically occurring normal polarity remanences are interpreted as an overprinted component imposed by the island’s terminal volcanic phase (the Feteiras Formation) now primarily exposed as strongly oxydized pyroclasts. The palaeomagnetic results are combined with available radiometric age estimates and local magnetic field information, and an integrated interpretation of all the data yields the principal conclusion that the Facho and Pico Alto volcanic sequences, covering the major part of the island, were laid down at around the Miocene/Pliocene boundary (— 5 Ma ago), i.e. immediately succeeding the local Messinian sedimentary horizon. A stable natural remanent magnetization (NRM) direction was obtained from most sites by stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization. The mean direction (excluding sites with intermediate NRM directions) is: D = 358.60, I = 64.00, a95 = 5.2°, N = 31. This gives a virtual geomagnetic pole (VGP) of 85.1 °N, 200.9 °E, which agrees well with the Late Tertiary apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Eurasia. A reverse—normal—reverse magnetostratigraphy is observed, which can be correlated with chrons 5Cr, 5C, and 5Br (17.6—15.2 Ma). Results of rock magnetic and reflected light microscopy studies indicate that titanomagnetite and its oxidation products are the main magnetic phases present. The grain size and degree of deuteric oxidation varies considerably between sites, with the titanomagnetites of thin vesicular lava flows tending to be more oxidized than those in thick massive bodies. Paleomagnetic results of Tertiary sediments from Corsica: evidence of post-Eocene rotation. Phys. Earth Planet. Inter., 62: 97—108. Middle Eocene (Lutetian) and Lower to Middle Miocene (Burdigalian—Langhian) sediments from Corsica have been investigated in a paleomagnetic study to constrain the amount and timing of tectonic rotation of the Corsican block with respect to Sardinia and stable Eurasia. The sediments are generally characterized by weak and unstable magnetization, and only five Eocene and five Miocene sites Out of 23 sites sampled provided interpretable data. Our best estimate for the Eocene paleomagnetic field for Corsica suggests — 370 of counter-clockwise rotation, and no latitudinal change, with respect to stable Eurasia in post-Eocene time. The new palaeomagnetic data are seen in conjunction with previously published Upper Cretaceous results from the Sintra and Sines intrusive complexes. The resulting database gives entirely new perspectives for evaluating the plate tectonic history of the Peninsula in Upper Cretaceous—Lower Tertiary time. A two-phase rotation of the Iberian micro-plate, an anticlockwise one of — 40° followed by a clockwise one of — 70°, is clearly in evidence. The net clockwise rotation provided a major impetus for the compressive deformation in the Pyrenees and the Bay of Biscay, and led to extensive remagnetization of older rock formations in the northern regions of Ibena. Previous~palaeomagnetic conclusions, in favour of a single anticlockwise rotation of — 35°, supposed to be directly connected with the formation of the Bay of Biscay, appear to be artefacts which stem from an incorrectly adopted palaeomagnetic reference frame. 1. The new palaeomagnetic data are seen in conjunction with previously published Upper Cretaceous results from the Sintra and Sines intrusive complexes. The resulting database gives entirely new perspectives for evaluating the plate tectonic history of the Peninsula in Upper Cretaceous—Lower Tertiary time. A two-phase rotation of the Iberian micro-plate, an anticlockwise one of — 40° followed by a clockwise one of — 70°, is clearly in evidence. The net clockwise rotation provided a major impetus for the compressive deformation in the Pyrenees and the Bay of Biscay, and led to extensive remagnetization of older rock formations in the northern regions of Ibena. Previous~palaeomagnetic conclusions, in favour of a single anticlockwise rotation of — 35°, supposed to be directly connected with the formation of the Bay of Biscay, appear to be artefacts which stem from an incorrectly adopted palaeomagnetic reference frame. 1. Palaeomagnetic results from 20 volcanic sequences and 11 intrusive bodies (sills and dykes) of the Serra Geral Formation (Paraná Basin) are reported in this paper. The sequences are widespread all over the basin, while sills and dykes (Ponta Grossa arch) come from the northeastern portion. The early Eocene Metchosin Complex is an ophiolitic sequence and is the northernmost part of the Crescent Terrane. It was underthrust beneath Wrangellia later in the Eocene. Directions of magnetization in sheeted diabase (layer 2) and gabbroic intrusions (layer 3) from the complex are internally consistent, and both normal and reversed polarities are present. Mean directions, irrespective of sign, differ not only from the expected Eocene palaeofield but also from one another. The palaeomagnetism of the older volcanic complex of Santiago constitutes a multicomponent structure, and magneto- mineralogical evidence suggests that the various remanence vectors are carried principally by titanomaghaemites. When viewed in the context of the African palaeomagnetic reference frame the predominant magnetization is consistent with an Upper Tertiary age, but two older magnetizations of inferred Lower Tertiary age are also in evidence. The demonstrable secondary nature of all three palaeomagnetic axes (each of them represented by both polarities) makes it likely that the actual emplacement of the older complex is of pre-Tertiary age, being probably an integral component of the pronounced tectonomaglnatic uplift phase that affected the entire northwest African margin in Upper Cretaceous time. that erosional stripping accompanied the formation of the pebble marker. The pebble marker is best interpreted as a lag deposit. The stratigraphic coincidence does not necessarily signify the concurrence of a reversal with the formation of the marker horizon, but rather that the relationship represents a variation on the unconformity test. The remanence in extrusive volcanic rocks of Lower Carboniferous (Visean) age in the Pennines of central England has been reinvestigated, employing detailed thermal demagnetisation and incorporating new geological knowledge of field relationships. A mean (reversed) direction of D/I = 203/36 ° (10 sites, R = 9.75) yields a pole position at 336°E 14°S (dp/dm ~ 6/10°). most prominent feature of the European palaeomagnetic record from Carboniferous rocks is a compact group of south poles plotting in the central-south Atlantic near to 340°E, 40°S (Piper, 1987). These poles are derived mostly from re- versed polarity magnetisations. Much direct and circumstantial evidence shows that they record a prominent overprinting event during late Carboni- ferous and Permian times which also dominates much of the older Palaeozoic data (Piper and Grant, 1989). A small number of studies from Lower Carboniferous rocks yield magnetisations with mixed polarities and poles removed from this group. Early stepwise thermal demagnetisation and analysis of magnetostratigraphy in the Kinghorn lavas from central Scotland (Wilson and Everitt, 0031-9201/91/$03.50 © 1991 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. All rights reserved 38 J.D.A. PIPER ET AL. 1963) implied that the Lower Carboniferous pole position actually lay near 330°C, 10°S. This result has been stubstantiated by later study (Torsvik et al., 1989) and if confirmed elsewhere will imply that Carboniferous times were characterised by appreciable apparent polar wander (APW) move- ment. They include investigations (Belshr, 1957; Clegg et al., 1957) made before cleaning methods were routinely employed. Subsequent studies (Everitt and Belshr, 1960) found evidence for primary remanence and ancient field reversal. The axis of remanence was oriented NE -/SW + contrasting with the typical southerly shallow-directed rema- nences in most other European Carboniferous rocks. Later unpublished studies include more ex- tensive sampling and alternating field (a.f.) de- magnetisation (Titman, 1971; Moyse, 1973)and thermal demagnetisation (Titman, 1971). They also recognised reversals of magnetisation and direc- tions divergent from remanence in contempora- neous limestones in northern England (Turner and Tarling, 1975; Turner et al., 1979). Unfortunately, both Titman and Moyse experi- enced difficulties in differentiating between lavas and intrusions and were not able to take ad- vantage of recent geological investigations (In- stitute of Geological Sciences, 1969, 1970, 1975a,b, 1976a,b, 1977a,b; Waiters and Ineson, 1981) clarifying the nature and stratigraphic position of outcrops in these poorly exposed rocks. The primary Lower Carboniferous pole positions accord with contemporaneous poles from the Midland Valley of Scotland and demonstrate that Carboniferous and younger tectonic movements are palaeomagnetically undetectable, at least between these two areas.
